steps.body:
Here is the sentence almost everyone gets wrong:

*"There is a 95% chance the truth is inside this interval."*

The truth is a fixed number. It is either inside your interval or it is not — there is no chance about it. The 95% describes the **method**: run it many times and about 95% of the intervals it makes will capture the truth.
Each bar is one poll's interval. The dashed line is a truth you would never actually get to see.

widget.prompt: Find the width at which about 19 bars in 20 reach across the truth. Draw at least 20 bars at that width.
widget.successFeedback: About 19 in 20 bars caught the truth. Notice what varied and what did not: the bars jumped around, the truth never moved. The 95% is a property of the bar-making machine.
widget.wrongLevelFeedback: Count the misses at this width. The 80% setting misses about 1 time in 5 — far too often. The 99% setting almost never misses, but its bars are so wide they say very little.
widget.moreIntervalsFeedback: A handful of bars cannot show a hit rate. Add more — a 95% claim is a claim about the long run.

cml.actionGoal: Generate repeated confidence intervals and coordinate method capture rate with confidence level and width.

explanationVariants: The parameter is fixed; the interval is random. So the probability statement belongs to the interval-making procedure, not to the parameter.
About 19 of every 20 intervals this method builds will contain the truth — which says nothing about whether the one on your screen is among them.

widget.prompt: You compute one 95% confidence interval: 44% to 52%. What may you say?

options.label: The method that produced this interval captures the truth about 95% of the time.
options.feedback: Right. Confidence is a track record of the procedure, and you are borrowing it for this one run.

options.label: There is a 95% probability the true value lies between 44% and 52%.
options.feedback: The true value is a fixed number, not a random one. It is already in or already out — this interval either caught it or it did not.

options.label: 95% of the population supports the proposal.
options.feedback: That confuses the confidence level with the estimate. The estimate here is around 48%; the 95% is about how reliable the method is.

options.label: 95% of samples would give an estimate between 44% and 52%.
options.feedback: Close but different: the guarantee is about intervals CAPTURING the parameter, not about future estimates landing in this particular interval.

steps.body:
Raising the confidence level widens the interval. There is no free lunch:

**99%** — catches the truth almost always, but the band may be so wide it rules nothing out.
**80%** — a tight, decisive-looking band that misses one time in five.

95% is a convention, not a law of nature. It is a chosen trade between being right often and saying something useful.

widget.prompt: Keep the sample at 80 and move the width selector to 99%. Draw at least 20 bars, then compare their LENGTH with the 95% bars you just made.
widget.successFeedback: Almost every bar reaches the truth now. Look at what it cost: each bar spans a far wider stretch of the axis than its 95% counterpart did, from exactly the same 80 people. Reliability and precision are traded against each other, and only a bigger sample buys both.
widget.wrongLevelFeedback: This run is still at a different width. Set the selector to 99% and draw again — the comparison this step asks for is between one width and another, so the setting has to be the one named.
widget.moreIntervalsFeedback: A handful of bars cannot show a capture rate. Draw at least 20 at this width: a 99% claim is a claim about the long run, not about one poll.

explanationVariants: Higher confidence needs a wider net, so the interval grows. Certainty and precision pull against each other.
You can always be 100% confident by saying "between 0% and 100%" — perfectly reliable, perfectly useless.

widget.prompt: You switch a report from 95% confidence to 99% confidence, keeping the same sample. What happens to the interval?

options.label: It gets wider — more confidence costs precision.
options.feedback: Right. To miss less often you must cast a wider net, and a wider net excludes fewer possibilities.

options.label: It gets narrower, because you are more confident.
options.feedback: Confidence is not conviction. A higher hit rate requires a bigger target, so the interval must grow.

options.label: It stays the same; only the label changes.
options.feedback: The multiplier changes with the level (about 1.96 at 95%, about 2.58 at 99%), so the arithmetic really does widen the band.

options.label: It gets narrower because 99% is closer to certainty.
options.feedback: Closer to certainty means a wider band, not a tighter one. The only way to have both is a bigger sample.

explanationVariants: A bigger sample narrows the interval at the same confidence. A higher confidence widens it at the same sample. They are separate dials.
The only way to be both more confident and more precise is to collect more data.

widget.prompt: Match each change to what it does to the interval.

right.label: half as wide, same hit rate
wider, and it misses less often
narrower, and it misses more often

pairErrors.feedback: Going UP in confidence cannot make the interval narrower — a higher hit rate needs a wider net.
More data buys precision without giving up the hit rate. That is the only lever that improves both.

widget.missFeedback: Sample size changes the width for free. Confidence level trades width against hit rate.
widget.successFeedback: Only more data improves both. Everything else is a trade.

hints: Check each sentence for a probability claim attached to the TRUTH rather than to the method.
The parameter is a fixed number. Any sentence that gives it a probability of being somewhere is suspect.
Two of the four sentences are fine, one is about the long-run behaviour of the procedure, and one puts the randomness in the wrong place.
explanationVariants: "There is a 95% chance the true value is in this interval" gives a probability to a fixed constant. The randomness lives in the interval, not in the truth.
Rewrite it correctly: 95% of the intervals produced by this method contain the true value. This is one of them, or it is not.

widget.prompt: A 95% interval comes out as 44%–52%. Which statement is WRONG?

options.label: "There is a 95% chance the true value lies between 44% and 52%."
options.feedback: Right — this is the wrong one. The true value is fixed; it does not have a 95% chance of being anywhere. The 95% belongs to the method.

options.label: "If we repeated this poll many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true value."
options.feedback: That one is exactly right — it describes the long-run behaviour of the procedure, which is what the level means.

options.label: "Values outside 44%–52% are less plausible given this sample."
options.feedback: That is a fair reading of the interval as a set of plausible values, and it makes no probability claim about the parameter.

options.label: "This interval either contains the true value or it does not — we just don't know which."
options.feedback: That is precisely the honest position. It sounds unhelpful, but it is what a fixed parameter and a random interval imply.

steps.body: Confidence is a property of the method.
takeaways: The parameter is fixed; the interval is random. So "95%" describes how often the METHOD captures the truth.
Any one interval either contains the truth or it does not — you are borrowing the method's track record.
Higher confidence means a wider interval. Only more data improves confidence and precision together.
steps.teaser: Next: two candidates, two bands, and the word "lead" doing more work than it can bear.

concept.body: Think of a machine that stamps out intervals. About 19 in 20 of its intervals contain the truth. You pull one out of the machine. You cannot say your interval has a 95% chance of being right — you can say the machine is right 95% of the time, and you trust the machine.

explanationVariants: It lives in the procedure — the long-run hit rate of intervals it builds.
It does not live in the parameter, which is a fixed number with no probability attached.

widget.prompt: The "95%" in a 95% confidence interval is a statement about what?

options.label: The method — 95% of the intervals it builds capture the truth.
options.feedback: Right. You inherit the method's reliability; the individual interval has no probability of its own.

options.label: The true value — it has a 95% chance of being inside.
options.feedback: The true value is fixed. It is inside or it is not, and no probability attaches to a constant.
